summary: Documents experience from Yeti DNS, an experimental, non-production root server testbed where technical and operational experiments can be run without risking the production root servers. It records what was learned deploying such a system.

eli5.summary: A practice playground for the internet's phone book, where people can test changes without breaking the real one.

questions: how does yeti test dns changes
subtitle: A global testbed for experimenting with DNS root server changes safely.

tldr.problem: The root servers handle critical internet infrastructure, making it nearly impossible to safely test changes or conduct experiments. Researchers need a way to test DNS innovations without risking production systems.
tldr.mechanism: Yeti DNS is a non-production root server testbed that mirrors the real root system but serves only known, volunteer participants. It replicates the production architecture with 25 servers across the world while allowing structural experiments like IPv6-only operation and multiple independent DNSSEC signers.
tldr.outcome: Yeti proved invaluable for testing IPv6-only operations, DNSSEC key rollovers, large response handling, and zone distribution mechanisms. It exposed software bugs and demonstrated that several experimental approaches work reliably, informing future root server improvements.

today: RFC 8483 is an Informational document published in October 2018, documenting the Yeti DNS testbed experience. The testbed remains active and continues to serve participants interested in DNS research and root server innovation. It has not been obsoleted or superseded.

sections.title: The Challenge of DNS Root Server Evolution
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) root servers handle a critical, high-stakes part of the internet. They answer queries that tell resolvers which servers hold information about top-level domains like .com or .org. Because of this responsibility, any change to root servers requires extreme caution. Proposals for innovation—using only IPv6, deploying DNSSEC with multiple signers, or testing new key rollover procedures—cannot be tested safely in production.

From 2015 onwards, a group of volunteers coordinated by the Beijing Internet Institute, the WIDE Project, and Paul Vixie's engineering team conceived Yeti DNS: a non-production testbed that mirrors the root server system but belongs entirely to participants who opt in. The testbed replicates the full root zone from IANA, applies only the structural changes needed for the testbed to function independently, and allows researchers to propose and run controlled experiments.
sections.eli5: Testing new ideas on the real root servers is dangerous, like testing a skateboard trick on a crowded bridge. Yeti is a practice park where engineers can try new tricks safely.

sections.title: Testbed Infrastructure and Design
sections.content:
Yeti follows the structure of the production root system but with deliberate differences for experimental control. The testbed includes three Distribution Masters (DMs), operated by BII, WIDE, and TISF, which retrieve the current root zone from a production root server (F-Root) on a staggered schedule. Each DM polls every 20 minutes, offset to distribute the load: BII at :00, WIDE at :20, and TISF at :40 past each hour.

Each DM transforms the retrieved root zone by replacing the production root server names and addresses with Yeti-Root server names and addresses, then signs the transformed zone. The zone is distributed via NOTIFY messages to 25 volunteer-operated Yeti-Root servers spread globally (in 2018). Recursive resolvers participate by configuring their hints file and DNSSEC trust anchors to use Yeti-Root servers instead of production servers.

All Yeti-Root servers are IPv6-only; they have no IPv4 addresses. This deliberate constraint allows testing whether an IPv6-only root infrastructure could survive critical scenarios, as part of broader internet transition planning. The testbed also uses free-form server names (like bii.dns-lab.net) instead of the single-letter abbreviations (A through M) of production root servers, avoiding DNS label compression optimizations and allowing researchers to observe how modern DNS handles larger priming responses.
sections.eli5: Three offices update the phonebook every 20 minutes, then send it to root servers around the world. The servers use only the IPv6 internet (the new kind) and have longer names so researchers can test how resolvers handle bigger answers.

sections.title: DNSSEC Innovation: Multiple Signers and Key Rollovers
sections.content:
A core Yeti experiment was testing multiple, independently operated DNSSEC signers. Unlike production, where a single authority signs the root zone, Yeti allows each DM to maintain its own Zone Signing Key (ZSK) while sharing a single Key Signing Key (KSK). This approach, called the 'Unique ZSK per DM' model, reduces the need to distribute secret key material and tests whether resolvers can reliably validate responses signed by different keys, all trusted through a single KSK signature over the DNSKEY record set.

The testbed conducted three DNSSEC Key Signing Key (KSK) rollovers, mirroring—and refining—ICANN's production KSK rollover plan. One rollover deliberately bypassed the RFC 5011 holddown timer to observe how resolvers failed (some required manual intervention). Another discovered a bug in BIND 9.10 where KSK rollovers failed for resolvers with multiple views if managed-keys was not configured in every view. A third measured the operational impact of large DNSKEY responses (up to 1975 octets) during concurrent ZSK and KSK rollovers, using RIPE Atlas probes to test over 230,000 IPv6 endpoints.
sections.eli5: Different offices can sign parts of the phonebook with their own keys, as long as they all trust a master key. Yeti tested this and found bugs in resolver software that production had never stressed before.

sections.title: IPv6-Only Operation and Fragmentation
sections.content:
Operating a root system on IPv6 alone exposed IPv6-specific challenges unseen in dual-stack production infrastructure. DNS responses from Yeti servers can exceed the minimum IPv6 MTU of 1280 octets, causing fragmentation. In one measurement using RIPE Atlas, when DNSKEY responses reached 1975 octets (during a KSK rollover), a 6.87% failure rate was observed—meaning nearly 7% of IPv6-capable endpoints could not receive the fragmented response. Smaller responses of 1414 octets showed a 2.47% failure rate, and even 1139-octet responses had a 0.42% failure rate, suggesting that middleboxes (firewalls, routers) aggressively drop IPv6 fragments.

TCP zone transfers between DMs and Yeti-Root servers also suffered from fragmentation issues. On some systems (NetBSD, FreeBSD, and specific VMware configurations), negotiated TCP Maximum Segment Size (MSS) reached 1440 octets despite socket options requesting the IPv6 minimum of 1280. Segments exceeding 1280 octets were dropped, causing transfer failures. Mitigation required manually setting TCP MSS to 1220 octets (1280 minus 60 bytes for IPv6 and TCP headers).

Despite these challenges, real-world end-users—even those with only IPv4 connectivity—could resolve names through Yeti using dual-stack resolvers. One participant deployed IPv4-to-IPv6 translation (IVI) to map Yeti-Root servers to IPv4 addresses for IPv4-only end-users, demonstrating the testbed's flexibility.
sections.eli5: IPv6 packets break into fragments when messages get too big, and many firewalls drop fragments. Yeti learned the hard way that 7% of the internet struggles with large IPv6 responses, and had to adjust TCP settings on some servers.

sections.title: Zone Distribution and Synchronization Challenges
sections.content:
With three independent DMs, each signing zone data with its own key, the Yeti-Root zone on each DM is functionally equivalent but not congruent—the signatures differ because each DM uses its own ZSK. This introduces a challenge for zone transfers: Incremental Zone Transfer (IXFR), the efficient mechanism for syncing zone changes, is unsafe between DMs because deltas would miss structural differences between incongruent zones. As a result, all Yeti-Root servers must use full zone transfers (AXFR), never IXFR, ensuring consistency.

Zone distribution also revealed timing issues. Although the staggered schedule was designed to ensure that at least one DM would have the latest root zone within 20 minutes, in practice Yeti-Root servers often lagged the root zone publication by 40 minutes or more. Some servers received a NOTIFY signal from one DM but then sent their SOA query and transfer request to a different DM that did not yet have the new zone. Better coordination or sticky master preferences could mitigate this, but it exposed that naive multi-master distribution requires careful design.
sections.eli5: With three offices signing different copies of the phonebook, you can't use a quick update method—you have to copy the whole book each time. And sometimes servers ask the wrong office, causing delays.

sections.title: Tools, Discoveries, and Future Directions
sections.content:
Operating the testbed produced practical tools now available to the community. YmmV (Yeti Many Mirror Verifier) captures DNS traffic sent to production root servers and replays it to Yeti servers, comparing responses to spot differences. PcapParser reassembles fragmented IPv6 datagrams and TCP segments from packet captures, essential for analyzing the fragmentation issues described above. DNS_ATR implements Additional Truncated Response (ATR), a technique to split large DNS responses at the application layer before IP fragmentation occurs. A hints file auto-update tool uses DNSSEC-validated root NS records to automatically maintain resolver configuration, working because Yeti signs its server names (unlike production, where they are not signed).

The experience revealed implementation bugs: Knot DNS 2.0 incorrectly compressed the root domain label with a pointer, increasing encoding size and breaking the Go DNS library. These discoveries led to fixes in both projects. Yeti also informed the design of ICANN's actual KSK rollover, and demonstrated that multiple ZSK signers, larger RSA keys, and alternative DNSSEC algorithms are operationally viable.

The testbed's mailing lists and GitHub repositories remain open, and no serious incidents have disrupted normal operation, suggesting that the experimental infrastructure is robust enough to serve its mission of informing real-world DNS evolution.
sections.eli5: Yeti created tools for comparing root servers, handling big packets, and updating resolver settings automatically. It found bugs in DNS software and proved that several new ideas actually work.
